extracted.intended_audience: philosophers, literary theorists, and literate readers interested in metaphysics and the theory of imagination
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length philosophical treatment that sets out foundational theses about truth, self-consciousness, and the genesis and role of the Imagination, intended as a model for constructive metaphysical argumentation and for relating poetic theory to philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: THESIS I — Truth is correlative to being
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge without a correspondent reality is no knowledge; if we know, there must be somewhat known by us. To know is in its very essence a verb active.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms a basic evaluative standard: a claimed knowledge must correspond to some reality; epistemic claims are active relations rather than passive labels. Use this to judge whether philosophical claims purport to refer to real correlates or are empty abstractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: THESIS II — Immediate vs mediate truth
rubrics_metrics.description: All truth is either mediate (derived from other truth(s)) or immediate and original. The latter is absolute (formula A. A.); the former is dependent or conditional (formula B. A.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argumentative criterion: avoid an infinite regress of derivation by identifying whether a proposition is presented as self-evident/immediate or as dependent. Beware of treating chains of dependent truths as if they supplied an ultimate ground; explicate which truths are claimed as primitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: THESIS III — Seek an absolute self-grounded truth
rubrics_metrics.description: We must seek an absolute truth capable of communicating to other positions a certainty it has not itself borrowed; a truth self-grounded, unconditional and known by its own light — a somewhat which is, simply because it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological standard for philosophical systems: demonstrate or argue for a self-standing principle that can serve as first ground. The description emphasizes that such a principle must be its own predicate and preclude the need for an antecedent cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: THESIS IV — There can be but one highest principle
rubrics_metrics.description: If there were two or more such principles, each must refer to some other by which its equality is affirmed; consequently neither would be self-established. Therefore there is but one such principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ontological/axiomatic criterion: avoid positing multiple independent ultimate principles. Use a priori argument to justify uniqueness and show how the discovered principle exhibits universal antecedence.

rubrics_metrics.name: THESIS V — The principle cannot be a 'thing' or merely a subject/object alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Such a principle cannot be any THING or OBJECT, nor can it be found in subject as subject or object as object; it must be the identity of both, since every thing presupposes some other thing and every object presupposes a subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphysical requirement: the first principle must overcome the subject/object dichotomy by being that which is neither purely object nor purely subject but their identity. Use this to judge candidate first principles for their ontological form.

rubrics_metrics.name: THESIS VI — The principle manifests in the SUM or I AM (self-consciousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: This principle manifests itself in the SUM or I AM (spirit, self, self-consciousness). In this, object and subject, being and knowing, are identical; the subject becomes object to itself in a perpetual self-duplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative standard for philosophical anthropology and epistemology: judge accounts of reality by whether they can be traced back to self-consciousness as the identity of subject and object. Emphasizes conceptualizing spirit as an act of self-objectification.

rubrics_metrics.name: THESIS VII — Self-consciousness implies act, will, and freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Intelligence or self-consciousness is impossible except by and in a will. The self-conscious spirit is a will; freedom must be assumed as a ground of philosophy and cannot be deduced from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative metaphysical criterion: any account of mind or intelligence should recognize volition as constitutive. Use this when evaluating theories that reduce consciousness to passive states — they fail to account for the active/volitional character.

rubrics_metrics.name: THESIS VIII — Spirit is neither purely finite nor infinite; life follows from reconciling the contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever in its origin is objective is necessarily finite; the spirit cannot originally be finite nor purely a subject; it must be the union of both, and in the existence, reconciling, and recurrence of this contradiction consists the process and mystery of production and life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for metaphysical models of personhood and becoming: prefer accounts that allow a dynamic reconciliation of opposing predicates rather than collapse into pure finitude or pure infinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: THESIS IX — The will/self-duplication is the mediate principle of sciences and immediate for transcendental philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: This principium commune essendi et cognoscendi, as subsisting in a WILL or primary act of self-duplication, is the mediate principle of every science and the immediate principle of transcendental philosophy. Theses refer to the subjective pole; the objective pole is left to natural philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological guidance: distinguish poles (subjective vs objective) and acknowledge that transcendental philosophy starts from self-consciousness as immediate ground. Use this to evaluate whether a discipline properly situates itself on the subjective or objective pole.

rubrics_metrics.name: THESIS X — Seek the last in our knowing within knowing (transcendental method)
rubrics_metrics.description: The transcendental philosopher does not inquire after an ultimate ground outside our knowing but asks what is last within our knowing itself; the act of self-consciousness is for us the source and principle of all possible knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epistemological standard: restrict inquiry to what can be known within our cognitive standpoint and justify turning to self-consciousness as the fixed point. Reject attempts that require passing beyond the principle of self-consciousness without decisive reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use technical terms when they prevent confusion and assist memory
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of technical terms in philosophy is justified whenever they tend to preclude confusion of thought and assist memory by exclusive singleness of meaning more than they bewilder by strangeness. Examples: using 'multeity' for kind abstraction, 'potence' to express a specific degree of power, or the coined verb 'potenziate'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style guideline: coin or adopt technical vocabulary only when no existing term is adequate and when the term's precision serves the argument. Legitimate neologisms must accord with the end of clear thought; avoid novelty for its own sake. The author defends specific coinages with examples and categorical criteria (convenience of scholastic phrase, correspondence in sound, avoidance of circumlocution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer precision over avoiding unfamiliar language; vagueness is worse than neologism
rubrics_metrics.description: Unusual and new-coined words are doubtless an evil; but vagueness, confusion, and imperfect conveyance of our thoughts are a far greater evil. Many reject concepts because their representation is impossible for intuition, not because the concepts are invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial and argumentative rule: when choosing between a precise but unfamiliar term and an imprecise familiar phrase, opt for the precision that secures clear conceptual boundaries. Be ready to justify terms against charges of pedantry by demonstrating conceptual necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and address different reader prejudices and classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers include practical men who require evident utility, religiously alarmed readers who fear metaphysical subversion of faith, and fellow metaphysicians attached to prior nomenclature. Address each: demonstrate utility, show that true metaphysics is allied with true divinity when relevant, and expose vagueness in prevailing terminology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience strategy: tailor responses to predictable objections—appeal to utility for pragmatic readers (Lord Bacon), defend metaphysics' compatibility with religion for sensitive readers, and argue terminological insufficiency to those wedded to inherited nomenclature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the popular/eclectic 'aphorisming' that lacks system
rubrics_metrics.description: The worst impediment is the predominance of a popular philosophy that dismisses system and logical connection, picking whatever is showy and plausible. This leads to loss of taste for system and substitutes echoing praise or blame for genuine argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria for evaluating philosophical prose: prize systematic unity and logical connection; judge negatively works that are merely eclectic aphorisms or stylistically plausible but substantively disconnected. Favor disciplined structure over showy fragments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Imagination from Fancy (functional differentiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to aggregate and associate (evoke and combine) belongs as well to Fancy as to Imagination; the author denies that aggregation/association alone constitutes Imagination. A man may use both tools simultaneously but the effect of each is distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing poetic or cognitive faculties, require clear functional definitions: do not conflate aggregation/association (fancy) with the higher esemplastic power (imagination). Evaluate literary or psychological claims by checking whether the alleged faculty's operations and outputs are properly distinguished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive method: combine discursive reasoning and intuition (mathematical analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosopher should use discursive reasoning to form schemes and then 'elevate the thesis from notional to actual' by intuitively contemplating the assumed power and its forces. The mathematical method (borrowing concepts like negative quantities) offers a fruitful analogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological rubric: develop a notional scheme via argument, then verify or manifest it through intuitive construction/representation. Use analogies from mathematics where applicable to clarify relations of opposites and their products; be explicit about when the move is heuristic (analogy) versus demonstrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model Imagination as the interpenetration of two indestructible contrary forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a nature with two contrary forces (centrifugal and centripetal), both alike infinite and indestructible; their essential counteraction (not mere opposite directions) yields a tertium aliquid — a finite generation or interpenetration — which is the source of imaginative production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theoretical criterion for a metaphysical account of imagination: prefer models explaining creative synthesis as the dynamic result of opposing but productive forces. This supplies an explanatory schema for how finite phenomena (works, forms) emerge from infinite tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy's two-fold function: reconcile reason with common sense and elevate common sense into reason
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the two-fold function of philosophy to reconcile reason with common sense and to elevate common sense into reason. Reject attempts that merely defend a blind realism or an empty metaphysical theater of apparitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative aim: philosophical systems should vindicate and refine common human judgments rather than replace them with speculative fictions; evaluate proposals by their success at making common sense intelligible within reasoned systems.
